stem: Which quotation from The Glass at Ferrow Head most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In Margaret Ilsley's 1894 novel The Glass at Ferrow Head, Hester Quayle keeps the weather records at her father's lighthouse on a stormy northern coast. The village fishermen forecast by signs, such as the color of the dawn or the behavior of gulls, while Hester's notebooks are filled with barometer readings. One critic argues that Ilsley presents Hester as relying on her instrument rather than on local lore even when its readings contradict what the sky itself appears to show: ______
choices: "The sky over the harbor was cloudless, and old Tobin swore by his knee that no blow was coming; but the glass had dropped since noon, and Hester went down to keep the boats in."
"Hester had learned to read the barometer before she could read her primer, and she put more faith in its needle than in any saying the fishermen had about gulls or red mornings."
"Black clouds were piling over Ferrow Head, yet the glass held perfectly steady, and Hester stood at the window a long while, unable to say whether she believed the needle or her eyes."
"The fishermen laughed at the brass barometer in the keeper's window, calling it the lady's clock and declaring that no needle ever made had smelled a storm before a gull did."
explanation: The claim has three parts that must all hold: Hester (1) acts on the barometer (2) instead of local lore, (3) even when the barometer conflicts with what the sky shows. Put choice A in plain words: the sky is clear and a fisherman's sore knee says no storm is coming, but the barometer is falling, so Hester tells the boats to stay in. The clear sky conflicts with the falling barometer, Tobin's knee stands for the lore, and Hester acts on the instrument. All three parts are there.

B.why: You matched the first half of the claim. Hester does trust the needle over the fishermen's sayings, but nothing in this line puts the barometer in conflict with what the sky looks like. You took the 'instrument over lore' part as the whole claim and dropped 'even when it contradicts the sky.'

C.why: You spotted the conflict between the sky and the barometer, which is the hard part of the claim, and stopped there. But in this line Hester can't decide which to believe. That works against a claim that she relies on her instrument. Finding the conflict isn't enough; she also has to act on the barometer.

D.why: This line comes from the right scene, with the barometer up against fishermen's lore, but it describes the fishermen's scorn, not anything Hester believes or does. The claim is about Hester, and she doesn't appear in this line.

stem: Which quotation from The Furrow Year most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Walter Brisco's 1923 novel The Furrow Year follows Ada Lunn, who takes over her late father's wheat farm and, on the advice of a county agent, begins planting clover in alternate years. Clover adds nitrogen to the soil, and the wheat sown in that field the following year draws on the stored nitrogen. A reviewer observed that over the course of the novel, Ada comes to value clover not for its own sake but for what it does for the wheat that follows it: ______
choices: "Ada, who had once thought clover a waste of good ground, came to love that acre for its purple heads and humming bees, though she knew it would never fill a single sack."
"Her father had called a clover field a field on holiday, and for years Ada had agreed with him, begrudging every acre she was obliged to leave out of wheat."
"The acre she had once grudged to clover now gave her the heaviest wheat on the farm, and Ada began to speak of the clover as if it were the first half of the wheat crop."
"The wheat on the east field came up thick and dark that June, taller than any Ada had ever grown, and the neighbors slowed their wagons at the fence to stare at it."
explanation: Break the claim into parts: Ada's view of clover (1) changes ('comes to value'), (2) she values it because of what it does for the next wheat crop, and (3) she does not value it for itself. In plain words, choice C says that the field Ada once resented losing to clover now grows her best wheat, and she starts treating the clover as part of the wheat crop. 'Once grudged' shows the change. Treating clover as 'the first half of the wheat crop' shows she values it only for what it does for the wheat. All three parts are there.

A.why: You saw that the claim describes a change of mind, and this line does show one. But Ada comes to love the clover for its flowers and bees, which is valuing it 'for its own sake,' the very reason the claim rules out. It even says the clover will never 'fill a sack,' so no crop benefit is involved. The tone fits; the reason is the opposite of the claim's.

B.why: This line shows only Ada's earlier view, when she resented clover as lost wheat ground. It is the starting point the claim describes moving away from. Nothing here shows her coming to value clover at all.

D.why: You brought the passage's nitrogen chain into the line. The wheat is impressive, but the quotation never mentions clover or what Ada thinks of it. It's the clover-to-wheat link and Ada's changed view that the claim needs, and you had to add both yourself.
